title: How Anthropic Builds: Lessons from Labs — Mike Krieger, Anthropic
talk_summary: Mike Krieger describes how Anthropic internally shifts from step-by-step task delegation to goal-level delegation, uses multiplayer async agent tagging (Claude Tag) as the dominant workflow, and is bottlenecked on human review of large AI-generated PRs. He also covers org design for fast prototyping (two-week persevere/pivot reviews, bet leads without direct reports) and pragmatic engineering habits like pre-measuring metrics and runtime config/flags.

takeaways.technique: Intent-and-tradeoffs review artifact instead of line-by-line diff review
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of sending a 2,000-line PR, authors share an artifact explaining intention, trade-offs, and the questions a reviewer would ask; the reviewer then interrogates the agent about the code rather than reading every line.

takeaways.technique: Goal-level delegation instead of step decomposition
takeaways.what_they_do: Shift from breaking work into steps to describing the end state, letting the agent work and surface trade-offs/questions, then reviewing where it landed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: moving to much more of the paradigm of I'm going to describe the goal, like go off and work on it

takeaways.technique: Two-week persevere-or-pivot review cadence with explicit shutdown
takeaways.what_they_do: Every project goes up for review each two-week cycle and is explicitly continued, pivoted, or shut down; shutdown is framed as the intended outcome, not failure.
Each initiative has a directly responsible individual who coordinates a cross-functional pod but does not manage those people, so pods can disband without reorgs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is the concept of a bet lead or a directly responsible individual... they don't manage usually any of the other people

takeaways.technique: Give agents a real VM with bash to escape tool limits
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than constraining agents to fixed tools, give them a VM that can write and run scripts when a built-in tool fails (e.g., PDF parsing), so they can self-remediate.
takeaways.evidence_quote: does every single like knowledge worker need a virtual machine that can write bash? Like, on the face of it, no, but then... it can remediate an issue

takeaways.technique: Pre-measure metrics and first-class runtime config/flags
takeaways.what_they_do: Instrument everything you might need before an incident, and make runtime configuration and rollout flags changeable in seconds as a first-class capability.
